pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Magnetic Fields

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion'; 'magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines'; 'Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5] (qualitative evidence; DCI PS2.B — forces that act at a distance can be explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal, age 11-12). The leap from KS2 is from an observable attract/repel RULE to an abstract FIELD MODEL: the magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where it exerts a force, represented by directed field lines (north-seeking → south-seeking, never crossing, closer spacing = stronger), and REVEALED — not created — by a plotting compass or iron filings. Qualitative only; includes Earth-as-a-magnet, the compass, and navigation. No quantitative field strength.
bestPractices: Start with a plotting COMPASS, not iron filings: the compass reveals field DIRECTION (the needle lies along the line, pointing north-seeking → south-seeking), which pupils need before the filings' clumped strength pattern.

Keep returning to the core idea that the field is the space where a force acts — iron filings and compasses only PROBE that space, they don't make the field 'more real'; stress the field is 3D, not merely the flat textbook pattern.
Don't assume the pattern is obvious: explicitly model drawing field lines (continuous, arrowed north→south, never crossing, spacing showing strength) and guide pupils on what to look for.
Scaffold the representation: draw small magnets → small compasses → omit the compass box and leave just an arrow, so the field-line abstraction is built up.

Treat the compass as a tiny magnet that aligns with Earth's field for navigation; the fact that Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole is really a magnetic south pole is enrichment, not essential at KS3.
Elicit pupils' own sentence on what 'magnetic field' means to surface wrong-track thinking, and carefully separate magnetic from gravitational and electric fields.
keyRepresentations: Plotting compass moved step-by-step around a bar magnet to trace a single field line
Bar-magnet field diagram: arrowed lines north→south, symmetrical, non-crossing, spacing = strength
Compass → arrow symbol progression for representing field direction
Iron-filings pattern (shape and strength) shown alongside the compass (direction)
Earth drawn as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to it (navigation)
commonMisconceptions: 'The field IS the iron filings / lines' — the lines are a representation; the field is a continuous region of force filling 3D space (IOP).
'The field exists only at the poles' or 'lines come out of the centre of the magnet' (Oak).
Drawing field lines that cross, or that have no direction/arrows.
Conflating the magnetic field with the gravitational or electric field because all 'act at a distance' (IOP; Bradamante & Viennot).
'Magnets need air/a medium to work' — the force acts through a vacuum (IOP).
Pole-labelling/reversal errors in attraction-repulsion diagrams (KS3 assessment analysis); carried-over 'all metals are magnetic / aluminium is magnetic'.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, build the leap from the KS2 attract/repel rule to the abstract FIELD MODEL: a magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where it exerts a force, revealed (not created) by a plotting compass or iron filings, and represented by directed field lines running north-seeking → south-seeking, continuous, never crossing, with closer spacing meaning stronger. Treatment is qualitative only (no field-strength numbers) and includes Earth-as-a-magnet, the compass and navigation. The anchor activity is a hands-on/screen field-MAPPING task where learners probe the space with a compass and assemble field lines themselves; a drawing/prediction activity assesses the examined competency; a reference layer consolidates vocabulary; and a narrowly scoped 3D exploration addresses the real 'field is only the flat pattern' misconception.

activities.title: Map the field with a plotting compass
feedback: If arrows appear only near the poles: ask the learner to test positions directly out to the side and below/above the magnet. The needle lines up with the magnet's field there too, which shows the field surrounds the magnet in all directions, getting weaker with distance.

If field lines are drawn crossing or without arrows: remind that each point has one needle direction, so lines cannot cross and must carry an arrow (pointing the way the needle's north-seeking end points, from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole).
If the learner says 'there's no field between my lines': have them drop the compass into a gap — it still deflects, so the field is continuous and the lines are just a representation.
If densest lines are drawn at the centre of the bar: compare with the iron-filings pattern, which clumps at the POLES — closer lines mean stronger field.
activities.rationale: Reading a field as a directed map revealed by a probe is a build-and-recompute task; letting learners stamp compass directions that knit into field lines and superpose a second magnet makes the abstract field something constructed and manipulated, directly confronting 'field only at the poles' and 'the lines aren't real'. Starting with the compass (direction) before iron filings follows the recommended teaching order. This can be done at a real bench with a bar magnet, plotting compass and iron filings, or with a screen model offering the same probe-and-stamp interaction; a live-recomputing screen model adds the second-magnet reshaping and compass/iron-filings view toggle as optional ways to make the mechanism visible.
sourceClaims: The field is the space around a magnet where it exerts a force; iron filings/plotting compasses only reveal direction and strength, they don't make it more real; the field exists in 3D, not just the 2D textbook pattern; start teaching with a compass (direction) before iron filings; field patterns are far from obvious to pupils and must be explicitly modelled.

KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.

MS-PS2-5: conduct an investigation [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5] even though not in contact (qualitative); DCI PS2.B — forces at a distance explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet and note that it settles pointing north.

Position a bar magnet, then move the compass step-by-step to many positions around it; at each position draw a small arrow pointing the way the needle's NORTH-SEEKING end points — this is the field direction, running outward from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole.
Join the arrows to trace continuous field lines, working outward from one pole and around to the other.

Deliberately place the compass out to the SIDE of the magnet (not just near the poles) and record which way the needle points compared with when the magnet was absent. Near the magnet the needle lines up with the magnet's field, but with some magnet orientations that direction can match its original northward direction, so also try turning the magnet.
Overlay or compare an iron-filings pattern on the same magnet, noting that filings show shape/strength while the compass shows direction — two readings of one field.
Bring a second magnet nearby and re-map a few points to see how the whole pattern changes (like poles push lines apart, opposite poles link them).
activities.intendedInsight: The field is a continuous region of force filling the space all around the magnet, not something that exists only at the poles or only where a line is drawn; the compass and filings merely PROBE it. Direction and strength are two readings of one invisible field.

activities.title: Draw, predict and apply the field-line rules
feedback: Predicting 'nothing, it always points north' vs 'it swings to line up with the nearer, stronger field' reveals whether the learner sees the needle as a magnet responding to a field — use iron filings afterward to make the field visible.
For lines without arrows: each line has a direction (the way a compass's north-seeking end points, from the magnet's north pole to its south pole); add arrows and re-check.
For crossed lines: two directions at one point is impossible, so redraw so lines never meet.
For pole-labelling errors: the end where lines emerge is north; cross-check with needle directions nearby.
activities.rationale: Producing and predicting (not just recognising) exercises the examined KS3 competency — 2D field-line drawing, compass direction, and pole labelling. The predict-observe-explain prompt surfaces whether the needle is understood as a magnet responding to a field. Recognition-only multiple-choice items can check the rules but do not by themselves elicit independent drawing, so construction tasks are included.
sourceClaims: KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Trace a field line through a marked point on a bar-magnet diagram, and at several marked positions draw the direction a compass needle would point.
Predict which way a compass will swing when placed at a given point near the magnet, then check against a plotted pattern.
Decide whether drawn field lines obey the rules: Do any cross? Do they carry arrows? Does spacing show strength?
Label the poles of a magnet from an unlabelled field pattern.
Predict-and-explain (predict, observe, explain): a compass far from magnets points north; predict what happens as a bar magnet is brought alongside it, and WHY, before testing.
activities.intendedInsight: Field-line drawing is a precise skill governed by rules (continuous, arrowed north→south, never crossing, spacing = strength), and the learner can predict a compass's behaviour from the field rather than treating it as a passive pointer.

activities.title: Earth as a magnet and the compass for navigation
feedback: If the learner says the needle is pulled toward the North Star, 'the cold', or 'north as a place': introduce Earth as a giant magnet with a field the needle aligns to, and deflect the needle with a bar magnet to prove the needle is itself magnetic.

Full understanding connects needle-as-magnet with Earth's field; a partial response states separate facts (Earth has a field; poles attract/repel) without explaining why the same end always points north.
The geographic-north/magnetic-south detail is enrichment; do not treat confusion about it as a core error at this stage.
activities.rationale: Earth's magnetism, the compass and navigation are statutory KS3 content and the standard explanation for 'why the needle points north'. Treating the compass as a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field unifies the pole rule with the field model. Spoken discussion of the transfer questions supports reasoning but the objective is the explanation, not dialogue for its own sake.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Draw the Earth as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to its field.
Explain why a compass needle's SAME end always turns to point north, in terms of the needle being a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field.
Reason about transfer: if you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?

Discuss the enrichment point: the Earth's magnetic pole near geographic north behaves like a magnetic south-type pole, so the needle's north pole is attracted to it (opposites attract) — flagged as enrichment, not required.
activities.intendedInsight: A compass works because the needle is itself a small magnet that aligns with Earth's magnetic field (when away from other magnets and iron), which is why the same end consistently points (magnetic) north and the compass can be used for navigation.

activities.title: Reference layer: the field-line rules at a glance
feedback: Treat this as a companion to the mapping bench: a finished diagram tells the learner the rules but does not let them probe with a compass or watch the pattern build, so use it after or alongside active mapping.
Tap-to-reveal regions can confirm rule-by-rule understanding; return to the compass whenever a learner doubts that the field fills the space.
activities.rationale: A tidy, labelled reference with tap-to-reveal explanations gives a reliable vocabulary and rule layer. Because it is fixed it cannot be probed, so it is positioned as a consolidation companion to the active mapping rather than the primary teacher — a fixed example can still teach the rules but cannot reproduce the field-as-revealed discovery.
sourceClaims: KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.
learnerActions: Consult a finished, labelled bar-magnet field diagram and reveal, region by region, the rules: lines run N→S, closer spacing = stronger, field strongest at the poles.
Reveal the Earth/compass link: Earth acts like a bar magnet and the compass needle aligns with its field.
Use this as a vocabulary and rule check-reference alongside the mapping activity.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the correct vocabulary and the field-line rules as a quick reference to support, not replace, hands-on probing.

activities.title: The field in three dimensions (narrow complement)
feedback: If a learner believes the field is only the flat pattern they drew on the table: have them hold the compass a short distance above the magnet and watch it still respond to the magnet, showing the field extends in all directions.
Keep this scoped to the 3D-nature point; the examined drawing, direction and navigation skills are fully served in 2D.
activities.rationale: The field genuinely is three-dimensional and 'the field is only the flat pattern' is a named misconception, so moving a probe through the surrounding space can address the 3D-nature point. This is proposed as a narrow complement, not the primary teacher, since the examined competencies are served in 2D; a physical exploration around a real magnet or a 3D screen model can both show the volume, each offering a different experience.
sourceClaims: The field is the space around a magnet where it exerts a force; iron filings/plotting compasses only reveal direction and strength, they don't make it more real; the field exists in 3D, not just the 2D textbook pattern; start teaching with a compass (direction) before iron filings; field patterns are far from obvious to pupils and must be explicitly modelled.
learnerActions: Move a compass or sensor through the space around a magnet at different heights and positions — above, below and to the sides — not just in the flat tabletop plane.

Record how the needle responds at each height and position close to the magnet (the effect weakens with distance), concluding the field occupies a VOLUME around the magnet, not only the flat textbook pattern.
Relate the 3D volume back to the 2D field-line diagram, recognising the diagram as one slice through the full field.
activities.intendedInsight: The magnetic field is genuinely three-dimensional — it surrounds the magnet in every direction — and the familiar 2D field-line diagram is one plane through that volume.

constraints: Keep treatment strictly qualitative at this stage: no numerical field-strength values.
Start with a plotting compass (direction) before iron filings (shape/strength); both only PROBE the field and do not make it 'more real'.
Field lines are a representation, not physical strings or the field itself; the field is a continuous region of force filling 3D space, present in the gaps between drawn lines.

Field-line rules to enforce: continuous, arrowed in the direction a compass's north-seeking end points (north-seeking → south-seeking, i.e. out of the magnet's north pole into its south pole), never crossing, closer spacing = stronger, field strongest at the poles (not the centre of the bar).
Carefully separate the magnetic field from gravitational and electric fields even though all 'act at a distance'; the magnetic force acts through a vacuum and does not need air/a medium.
Watch for carried-over errors: 'all metals are magnetic' / 'aluminium is magnetic', and pole-labelling/reversal mistakes in attraction–repulsion diagrams.
The Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole behaving as a magnetic south-type pole is enrichment, not essential at this level.
A fixed/labelled diagram is a reference scaffold: it cannot be probed with a compass and does not reproduce the field-as-revealed discovery, so pair it with active mapping.
Recognition-only items (e.g. rule multiple-choice) can check understanding of rules but do not elicit independent construction of a field diagram; include drawing/prediction tasks for that.

A persona/dialogue format does not itself elicit the compass-probing and field-line drawing that build and read a field map (those require hands-on or screen construction); discussion can still support reasoning about explanations such as why the needle's same end points north.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four sources (IOP Spark; Oak National Academy) are marked verified:false in the source row; claims attributed to them (including the 3D-nature misconception and the field-line rules) should be re-checked before relying on them as established.

The original recommendation asserted that the mapping bench conveys the field 'exactly what a static diagram cannot convey'. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources; it has been softened to a scoped affordance (fixed diagrams cannot be probed) rather than a universal law.

The source's framing that a quiz 'only assesses' and that 3D is uniquely necessary for the 3D point were softened: production/prediction tasks can teach, and both physical and screen 3D exploration can address the 3D-nature misconception.

Enrichment detail retained from the source: Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole is actually a magnetic south-type pole. This is a correct standard statement but can confuse at KS3; flagged as enrichment only.

The 'conversation' artefact was judged a poor fit in the source; its narrow point — that a dialogue format does not itself elicit the probing/drawing needed to construct a field map — is preserved as a constraint, without claiming dialogue cannot support related reasoning.

The field-direction/arrow convention was clarified in Activity 1 so the arrow points the way the compass's north-seeking end points (out of the magnet's north pole toward its south pole); an earlier ambiguous '(north-seeking end → south-seeking end)' phrasing could have been read as drawing the arrow the wrong way.

assess.poeTask: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet — it points north. Ask students to predict what happens as you slowly bring a bar magnet alongside it, and WHY, before doing it. Predicting 'nothing, it always points north' versus 'it swings to line up with the nearer, stronger field' reveals whether they see the needle as a magnet responding to a field; iron filings then make the field visible.
probeDeeper: Is there a magnetic field in the space between two field lines you've drawn? How do you know?
If you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?
Earth's magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole — is it a magnetic north or a magnetic south pole? How can you tell from the compass?
Where around the bar magnet is the field strongest, and how would iron filings show it?
assess.correctAnswer: The Earth has its own magnetic field. The compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with that field, so its north-seeking (north) pole always turns toward Earth's magnetic north. The same end points north because it is that end's north pole being pulled along the field toward Earth's magnetic north (which is actually a magnetic south-type pole, so opposites attract).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The needle points north because it's pulled toward the North Star / the cold / true north as a place.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce Earth as a giant magnet with a field the needle aligns to; deflect the needle with a bar magnet to prove the needle is itself magnetic.
errorPatterns.distractor: The needle is pulled toward the North Star, the coldest place on Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a non-magnetic cause; no mention of Earth's field.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Field lines are real strings, and there's only a field where I've drawn a line.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a plotting compass / iron filings to show the field is continuous everywhere around the magnet; lines are a representation, their direction = force on a north pole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there is no field in the gaps between drawn lines; treats the lines as physical objects.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The field is strongest in the middle of the magnet, between the poles.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iron filings show the field concentrated at the POLES; closer lines mean a stronger field.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws the densest field lines at the centre of the bar.

responseLevels.gap: Explains the compass by a non-magnetic cause (North Star, cold, 'north is up'), or thinks field lines are physical strings with nothing between them.
responseLevels.full: Explains the needle as a small magnet aligning with Earth's magnetic field so its north pole points to magnetic north, draws the field (with direction, strongest at the poles) as a representation of a continuous field, and transfers to navigation and other locations.
responseLevels.partial: States the pole rule and that Earth has a field, and can draw a bar-magnet field pattern, but treats these as separate facts — e.g. draws lines without direction, or can't say why the needle's same end points north (doesn't connect needle-as-magnet with Earth's field).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A compass needle settles pointing north wherever you put it in the room. What is making the needle point that way — and why does the SAME end always end up pointing north?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the field model attributes the alignment to the EARTH'S magnetic field acting on the needle-magnet everywhere in the room. A student without it invokes the needle being 'attracted to the North Pole/North Star' or 'to the cold', or thinks it only works near another magnet. Tier 2 — why the SAME end — forces them to treat the needle as a magnet with poles interacting with a field, not a passive pointer.
